subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a keel-billed toucan model using the SDK, thinking through realistic proportions—roughly 50-55cm body length with a large beak close to 40% of that, which I'll need to stylize appropriately for the scene.

For the branch and base, I'm working through how to satisfy the rule that the model's lowest points touch y=0—maybe a mossy branch angling diagonally down to the floor like a fallen limb, with the toucan perched partway up it, rather than something floating or needing an awkward support stub.

Branch as a horizontal sweep around y≈0.75m resting on the stump, toucan perched on top, with an orchid growing beside it from a short stalk. Estimating real-world scale: toucan body about 0.5m plus beak, branch around 0.9m long, total model height near 1.2m, with the body tilted and tail hanging down the back as is typical for a perched toucan. Setting up coordinates with feet at the branch top around y=0.78, branch center near y=0.72 with a tapered radius around 0.045 for a thick limb.

Refining the branch to taper to about 0.03 radius, with the stump rising from the floor to roughly y=0.6-0.66 where the branch overlaps its top, considering moss texture on the stump. For the toucan itself, I'm planning a glossy black capsule-like torso (#141414), a head sweeping forward off the neck, and a lemon-yellow (#ffd400) bib across the throat and upper chest consistent with keel-billed toucan coloring.

For the plumage, I'm deciding to paint the body using a per-texel function based on normal and position -- yellow where the normal faces forward and the point sits within the chest region, black elsewhere, with hard pixel-precise boundaries since all painted parts share one texture sheet. I'm also planning a scarlet patch (#e0202a) under the tail using a similar position-based paint condition targeting the rear-bottom area of the body.

Now I'm thinking through the eye: a lime-green bare-skin ring circling a dark pupil, which I could build either as a swept torus-like loop around the eye position on the head surface, or more simply as a decal using an SVG texture showing a green ring with dark iris and white highlight.

Actually, maybe a raised ring would look better than a flat decal for that "wow" factor, so I'm weighing a swept 3D ring versus a simple texture decal. For the overall structure I'm planning the branch first: bark with a sweep geometry, mossy patches painted on using mottled green-brown texture, and small clumps of moss scattered on the top surface using flattened low-poly spheres stuck onto areas where the surface normal points upward.

I'm figuring out how to properly scale the moss clumps and whether to paint texture directly onto the branch instead of adding separate moss cards, since paint functions can conditionally return different textures based on surface normal direction. For the stump, I'm considering a simple tapered cylinder with bark texture, positioned without a bone attachment so it defaults to the nearest joint.

Now I'm thinking through whether the branch needs to rest on something physical, since floating geometry doesn't fit the scene constraints requiring models to touch the ground or hang from above. A fallen log or tree stump resting on the floor seems like the most natural solution for the toucan's perch.

I'll build a mossy stump using a lathe shape with a flared base and rounded top, giving it a low-poly turned profile. The branch will sit with its underside slightly sunk into the stump's top surface, letting it appear to lie naturally across it.

For the orchid, I'm planning a pink phalaenopsis-style bloom with sepals, petals, and a darker labellum, built from extruded petal shapes radiating around a flower center with a green stem sweeping from the branch to the bloom.

I'm also thinking through the overall scene layout — placing the branch along the Z-axis so the toucan perches facing forward, with the orchid positioned beside it on the branch where it'll be visible to the viewer.

Working out branch taper and stump placement so the branch sits exactly on top with a slight sink, then positioning the toucan's feet at the branch's top surface with zygodactyl toes wrapping around it. I'm sketching the toucan's body proportions based on a real keel-billed toucan—body, tail, and the oversized beak length relative to total size.

Now I'm figuring out the perched posture: hip joint near the feet, legs bent down to the branch, and the spine chain running from the tail base up to the chest at an angled tilt so the head rises forward while the tail hangs back and down.

I'm working out the leg skeleton using IK limb chains, placing hip, knee, and ankle joints so the feet land on the perch, then naming each joint segment for the rig.

I'm working out the branch geometry near the center using catmull-rom points, and placing the orchid beside the toucan at roughly x=0.3 on the branch top, with the stump below at x=0. Then I'm setting the foot targets at (±0.05, 0.77, -0.02) so the toes wrap around the branch surface.

For the leg chains, I'm reasoning through avian anatomy -- the visible "knee" on a perched bird is really the ankle, with the true knee bending forward -- and setting up two-segment limb chains with lengths around 0.12 and 0.10, using a forward bend direction so the joint bulges correctly, parented to the hip joints on the body.

Now I'm starting to sketch out the full skeleton root structure: a hips joint positioned near (0, 0.99, -0.06) with orientation defined by an aim point, from which a spine chain running tail base to back to chest to neck will extend upward.

I'm plotting the spine as a curved path through four points rising from the tail base (0, 0.96, -0.2) up through rump, chest, to neck base (0, 1.2, 0.2), giving the perched toucan an upright posture. From the four points I get three span joints named spine1 through spine3, and I'm working out how the neck will continue from there.

I'm leaning toward having "hips" be the chain's first joint itself rather than a separate root — since the spec requires exactly one root joint with no parent, I can just let the spine chain's first joint serve as that root, naming it "hips" directly instead of adding a duplicate joint at the same position.

For the spine points I'm planning hips, back, chest, and a neck base, with the head joint attached as a separate child off the spine's tip joint so it can bend independently. The tail will also hang off the hips joint, branching downward and back from there.

Now I'm working out body shaping by sweeping stations of varying width and height along the spine path, tapering from a wider rump and chest down toward a narrower neck.

I'll derive the chain path from the same station coordinates used for the loft, so the body bends consistently with the skeleton. For the head, I'm considering a sphere-based part with scale adjustments to get the toucan's bulky head shape, attached to the head joint at the neck tip.

Since I'm unsure exactly how the scale parameter is formatted in the part options, I'll instead scale the sphere geometry directly before passing it in, since that's a safe operation. I'm also noting that without explicit orientation given, the part will default to world axes, and the geometry's own local orientation still moves with its parent bone during rigging.

For geometry already built in model space with translated or merged vertices, I can pass at: [0,0,0] alongside the bone so the mesh stays exactly where its vertices place it, without any extra orientation option needed. I'll construct the head geometry by translating and rotating it directly rather than relying on the part's positioning options.

I'm planning the beak as a separate articulated piece with its own jaw joint — an upper mandible rigidly attached to the head and a lower mandible attached to a jaw joint positioned at the hinge near the back of the beak, so the mouth can open.
